tip: 'Wohin' asks about direction, movement toward a place; 'wo' asks a fixed location: 'wohin fahren Sie'.
The prefix 'über-' is inseparable here, so 'überprüfen' never splits apart.
After 'ein' with a masculine noun, the adjective adds '-er' here: 'ein großer Vogel'.
'Unter' is a two-way preposition; for a static location it takes the dative: 'unter einem großen Baum'.
'In' is two-way; motion into something takes the accusative: 'in eine neue Wohnung'.
'Zum' is a contraction of 'zu dem': 'zum Frühstück'.
'Helfen' always takes a dative object: 'ihrer Mutter'.
The stray 'an' at the end belongs to 'anrufen' (to phone): 'ruft seinen Bruder ... an'. On its own, 'ruft' just means calls out or shouts.
'Heißen' means to be called, so 'wie heißen Sie' literally asks how you are called, that is, your name.
'Das Schloss' stays 'das' in the accusative – neuter articles don't change between nominative and accusative.
'Soll' here expresses an obligation set by someone else, what one is supposed to do: 'soll den Kamin reinigen'.
The verb stays in second position; start with a time phrase and the subject follows: 'nächste Woche beginnt der Deutschkurs'.
The genitive shows possession, of whom or what: 'unserer Kinder' means of our children.
'Steigen' marks a change of state, so its perfect uses 'sein', not 'haben': 'ist gestiegen'.
A recurring time expression goes in the accusative with no preposition: 'jeden zweiten Sonntag'.
'Nach' always takes the dative: 'nach dem Essen'.
'Jemandem gut tun' means to do someone good and takes the dative: 'tut dem kranken Kind gut'.
'Anfangen' pairs with 'mit' plus dative to say start with: 'mit dem neuen Projekt'.
A separable verb splits even in the simple past: 'einsortieren' becomes 'sortierte ... ein'.
'Stammtisch' is a German tradition – a regular table at a pub for a group of friends.
'Könntest du' is the polite could you, softer than the blunt 'kannst du' (can you). It turns a demand into a courteous request.
With the separable prefix 'aus-', the perfect's 'ge-' slots between prefix and stem: 'ausgelesen' is 'aus' + 'ge' + 'lesen'.
After the dative 'dem', the adjective flattens to '-en': 'dem alten Patienten'. The article 'dem' already shows the case, so 'alt' just takes '-en'.
In the accusative, 'der Mann' becomes 'den Mann' – only masculine articles change.
'Dem Briefträger' marks the receiver as dative: the to of to the mail carrier lives inside the article 'dem', not in word order or a preposition.
'Schwer' means hard or difficult here, not physically heavy: 'aller Anfang ist schwer' = every beginning is difficult.
'Fertig' means done or ready, and 'etwas fertig machen' means to finish it: 'ich mache das Abendessen fertig'.
With separable verbs, 'zu' slips between prefix and stem: 'wieder' plus 'sehen' becomes 'wiederzusehen', written as one word.
After a definite article the neuter adjective ends in '-e' here: 'das kaputte Fahrrad', never 'das kaputt Fahrrad'.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun the adjective takes '-es' here: 'ein schönes Bild'. The '-es' marks the neuter that 'ein' hides.
